# Jayaddisajātaka (Ja 513)

**ID:** Ja 513
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Jayaddisajātaka
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** Prince Victor
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/ja513

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Jayaddisajātaka* (Ja 513) is a canonical Pali birth story set in the kingdom of Kampilla (Uttarapañcāla) [Bareau; Fausböll 1891]. According to its introductory framework (*paccuppannavatthu*), the Buddha related the tale concerning a monk who supported his mother, noting that ancient sages surrendered their royal sovereignty to sustain their parents [SuttaCentral]. In the narrative of the past, an ogre-demon (*porisāda* / *rakkhasa*) terrorizes the region; this creature was originally a prince stolen as an infant and raised by a vengeful ogress (*rakkhasī*) in a cemetery to feed on human flesh [Sutherland 1991; DeCaroli 2004; Ohnuma 2012]. When King Jayaddisa is captured by the man-eating ogre on a hunting expedition, the king secures temporary release by promising to return after settling his royal duties [Bareau; DeCaroli 1999]. In his stead, his son Prince Alīnasattu—the Bodhisatta—voluntarily surrenders himself to the ogre [DeCaroli 1999; Fausböll 1891]. Through his utter fearlessness and adherence to virtue, the Bodhisatta exposes the ogre's true identity as King Jayaddisa's elder brother, reconciles the cannibal with his family, and guides him to renounce man-eating and become an ascetic [Bareau; DeCaroli 1999; DeCaroli 2004]. In the story's resolution (*samodhāna*), the man-eating uncle is identified as Aṅgulimāla, an elder ascetic as Sāriputta, and Alīnasattu as the Buddha himself [Nyanaponika et al. 2003; Fausböll 1891].

Scholars often analyze the tale alongside the *Mahāsutasomajātaka* (Ja 537) as preserving ancient Indian motifs of anthropophagy and the monastic conversion of demonized figures behaving like *yakkhas* [DeCaroli 2004; Migot]. The narrative also appears in the *Cariyāpiṭaka* (as the *Jayaddisacariya*) to exemplify the Bodhisatta's perfection of moral conduct (*sīlapāramī*) [Bareau], and is mapped against related stories in early Chinese translations such as the *Liudu jijing* [Trung Huynh 2016]. DharmaNexus identifies extensive Pali-internal text reuse (66 shared passages across 4 texts), dominated by the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* and the *Mahāsutasomajātaka* (14 matches, including §6.2–8.2 ↔ §38.1–40.2), along with alignments to the *Cariyāpiṭaka-aṭṭhakathā* [DharmaNexus].

**Parallels and text reuse**

- Text reuse within the Pali corpus (DharmaNexus): Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā (Catuttho bhāgo) (Atk S0513a4) (§16.1–19.4 ↔ §5641–5653); Mahāsutasomajātaka (Ja 537) (§6.2–8.2 ↔ §38.1–40.2); Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā (Pañcamo bhāgo) (Atk S0514a1) (§29.2–29.4 ↔ §4854); Cariyāpiṭaka-aṭṭhakathā (Atk S0512a) (§30.4–31.6 ↔ §1210–1213)
- Cross-language matches (DharmaNexus): འཕགས་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་མདོ། (ārya-mahāparinirvāṇa-nāma-mahāyāna-sūtra) (D0120) [bo]; འཕགས་པ་དཔལ་སྦས་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་མདོ། (ārya-śrīgupta-nāma-sūtra) (D0217) [bo]

- [DharmaNexus] DharmaNexus database — Identified Pali-internal matches with Ja 537, the Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā, and Cariyāpiṭaka-aṭṭhakathā.

- [DeCaroli 2004] Robert DeCaroli, Haunting the Buddha: Indian Popular Religions and the Formation of Buddhism (2004) — Detailed the background of the ogress and cannibalism motifs, comparing the conversion methods with Ja 537.
- [DeCaroli 1999] Robert Daniel DeCaroli, Haunting the Buddha (1999) — Provided summary of the plot involving Jayaddisa's capture, Alīnasattu's substitution, and the uncle's conversion.

- [Ohnuma 2012] Reiko Ohnuma, Ties That Bind: Maternal Imagery and Discourse in Indian Buddhism (2012) — Noted the demoness maternal motif in Ja 513 and the variant spelling Jayyadisa Jātaka.
